To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a higher dietary ratio of long-chain omega3 to total omega-6 fatty acids for prevention of COX- 2-dependent adenocarcinoma is a hypothesis that is supported by a number of epidemiological studies, but that further research is warranted.
the ratio of long-chain omega3 (EPA and DHA) to omega-6 fatty acids (arachidonate and its precursors) in the diet is inversely associated with risk for COX-2-dependent adenocarcinoma.
A higher dietary ratio of long-chain omega3 to total omega6 fatty acids is associated with lower risks of adenocarcinaomas of the colon, pancreas, and prostate.
In summary, our research is concerned with
elucidating the mechanisms by which the long-chain omega- 3s, abundant in fatty fish, can reduce risk for a number cancers.
the impact of dietary factors on the incidence and severity of cancer, with an emphasis on the role of omega-3 fatty acids.
the impact on human health of the dietary ratio of long-chain omega3 to omega-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA), with particular emphasis on the impact of this ratio on risk of colorectal cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no evidence of a protective effect of fish oil supplements against cancer risk.
there is a need for more research on fish consumption and cancer risk, and that the results of such studies would be of great value to public health.

a higher dietary ratio of long-chain omega 3 to total omega 6 fatty acids may be protective for COX-2-dependent adenocarcinoma, and that this effect may be mediated by the anti-inflammatory activity of EPA and DHA.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the long-term intake of fish, especially nonfried fish, is associated with a lower risk of colorectal cancer.

the evidence to date is consistent with the hypothesis that a higher dietary ratio of EPA/DHA to omega-6 fatty acids, achieved by regular consumption of fish and other seafood, can lessen risk for a wide range of COX-3-dependent adenocarcinoma.

there is no convincing evidence that fish or fish oil consumption is associated with an elevated risk for cancer of the breast, colon, or prostate, but there is some evidence for an association with a reduced risk.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ratio of EPA and DHA to arachidonate (and other omega-6) is the most important consideration in determining the impact of long-chain omega3s on cancer risk.

the ratio of EPA plus DHA to arachidonate (the ratio of long-chain omega−3s to total omega−6) in the diet is a key determinant of PGE2 synthesis, and that a higher ratio may have a meaningful protective effect on the risk for a number cancers.
the ratio of omega-3 to omega-6 fatty acids in the diet is a key factor in cancer risk, and a diet with a high proportion of long-chain omega3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA) is protective.
